prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and the experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B039 as a single-part prize, now with a narrower citation. Band topology gave condensed-matter physics a new organising principle: a Z2 invariant that protects edge and surface states against disorder and that can be computed for real materials with first-principles codes. The loop from prediction to measurement closed quickly and has held for about twenty years. Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall idea in 2005, and Molenkamp's group measured the quantized edge conductance in HgTe wells in 2007. Independent groups have since confirmed both the 2D and 3D cases, and the theoretical interpretation has not moved. The round-1 exchange sharpened my wording and left my ranking unchanged. A citation confined to the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, with the realisation in HgTe, is a bounded achievement. Kane and Mele supplied the invariant and the prediction, and Molenkamp supplied the observation that turned it into a physical effect. The 2016 prize covered Chern-number quantum Hall phases and topological phase transitions, not time-reversal-protected Z2 physics, so I do not think it narrows the room.
statement.case_against: The credit remains the weak point, and I do not want to minimise it. The HgTe experiment tested the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and not the original Kane-Mele graphene proposal, where spin-orbit coupling is far too small. Johansson and Danielsson are right that the citation must say so, and Molenkamp should be credited for the discovery and not for a prediction he did not make. Bernevig and Hughes are outside any three-name credit, and Zhang cannot be honoured posthumously. The 3D work of Fu, Moore, Balents, Roy, Hasan and Cava is a separate branch that a narrow citation leaves acknowledged but uncredited. A sceptical reviewer could say the committee drew the line to suit a trio. B022 has a cleaner two-name credit and I cannot deny that. I am also recalling the priority chronology from memory, and external expert reviews of BHZ and the 3D priority would properly come before a final vote.

responses.point: Danielsson proposes a B039 citation confined to the 2D case, with the BHZ and Hasan contributions handled through external-expert requests, and asks whether I regard the 3D case as a separate achievement or part of the same one.
responses.response: I now treat them as two achievements and I have adopted your wording. The 2D quantum spin Hall effect, with its Z2 classification and the HgTe observation, is bounded and has a defensible trio. The 3D case has its own theory (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Roy) and its own ARPES discovery (Hasan, Cava), and no three-person set covers both. I would not claim the whole field in the citation. I will not pretend this removes the BHZ problem: it only makes the citation honest about what the trio did. I agree that the Secretary should obtain external views on BHZ and Hasan before the final ballot.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that the attribution problem should be settled in the citation wording, so that the 3D case becomes an acknowledged adjacent achievement, and that a clock prize has a boundary against earlier prizes that no citation can remove. He also says B022 would win if precision were weighted above novelty.
responses.response: I agree on the wording and have changed my citation in that direction. Your point that the clock's overlap with 2005 and 2012 is structural carries weight with me. But I would not call it decisive, because the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct idea. On B035 you are right and I have changed my mind: the pairing mechanism is unresolved and I would let it wait, so I have dropped it from my alternatives. I replaced it with B025 because ultracold-atom quantum simulation also rests on a theory-experiment loop, but I would not claim it is mature in the way B039 is.

responses.point: Lindroth backs B022 for its single clear idea, independent reproduction at several laboratories and the tightest attribution, and in round 1 asked whether the ARPES line is better treated as a separate achievement.
responses.response: I have answered your question: the ARPES and 3D work is a separate achievement in my view. Your argument for B022 is strong on credit and reproducibility, which are the things I check first, and I accept that the magic-wavelength lattice is a real step beyond the comb and the ion clocks. My disagreement is about what the prize should reward. The clock has given a much smaller error bar and a series of consistency tests, and gravitational redshift over millimetres is a fine demonstration. Band topology changed what we think a phase of matter can be. I would still say that is the larger physical discovery. You are right that this is a judgement and not a proof, and I will not argue that your reading is unreasonable.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the committee can defend a quantum-spin-Hall-only citation without BHZ, and whether the 3D discovery is then stranded. He argues that the clock credit has no comparable gap.
responses.response: I think the answer is a qualified yes. A citation for the Z2 quantum spin Hall prediction and its observation in HgTe is defensible if it states the HgTe scope exactly. The 3D discovery is not stranded in the sense of being denied, since a later prize can still reach it. But I accept that any trio leaves out someone whose contribution was close to decisive, and that the clock does not have that problem. I weigh it as a cost and not as a disqualification. Your systematic-budget standard is the one I would apply to experiments, and the HgTe edge conductance has been reproduced by other groups, though at less than the 1e-18 level of precision.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B022 because she can be certain who did it first, and would move B039 up if the Kane-Mele Z2 step and the Molenkamp observation can stand alone as one achievement.
responses.response: Your condition is close to my revised proposal. The Z2 prediction (Kane and Mele) and the HgTe observation (Molenkamp) form a bounded 2D achievement, and the citation now says so. I do not claim it stands entirely alone, because the observation followed BHZ and I have said that openly. Where we differ is that you would rather award where the 'who first' question is cleaner. I give the original proposal and the physical discovery more weight than a tidy credit. I would not oppose B022 and have kept it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B022 after the openings and asks whether the committee can defend the three-name B039 split to expert reviewers. He defers on the condensed-matter merits.
responses.response: I cannot promise the split will go unchallenged, and I would not advise the committee to rely on my judgement alone. Your question for external reviewers is the right one. I would ask them specifically whether the Kane-Mele Z2 prediction plus the Molenkamp HgTe measurement is accepted as a coherent 2D achievement, and how they rate the BHZ contribution against it. If they judge BHZ decisive, I would have to reconsider and B022 would then be my preferred part. I note you moved to B022 partly because of the stronger support signal. I do not use support counts that way, but your reasons on the clock itself are sound.

uncertainties: Whether external experts would judge the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal decisive enough that a trio without Bernevig and Hughes is indefensible. If so I would move to B022.
Whether the committee accepts the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the 3D topological insulators as two achievements with a prize for the first only.
How far the 2016 prize narrows the room for a Z2 topological-insulator prize. I think little, but colleagues disagree.
The priority chronology is from memory and has not been verified from sources. I am also less certain of the B022 chronology.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate has emerged, and I have no stated personal or institutional tie to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori or Ye. I chaired the committee for the 2025 prize, which concerned circuits and so bears on B023, which I do not propose. Uppsala theory collaborates with MAX IV and ESS users, which does not touch any candidate.
